title: Momentum — mass in motion
examTip: Momentum calculations come up reliably in exams. p = mv is simple. But examiners also test conservation of momentum: in a closed system, total momentum before = total momentum after. They also test force as the rate of change of momentum (F = Δp/Δt). Always include units: kg m/s.
introTips: Momentum has direction as well as magnitude. It is a vector quantity. When things collide, momentum can be transferred from one object to another.
Conservation of momentum is the key idea. In any collision or explosion, total momentum before = total momentum after. This is true as long as no outside forces act.
Force × time = change in momentum. Compare a larger force for a shorter time with a smaller force for a longer time. Both can give the same change in momentum.
intro: Momentum measures how hard it is to stop something that is moving. A slow lorry can have the same momentum as a fast car. Stopping either one in the same time takes the same force. In a closed system, momentum is conserved in collisions and explosions. That makes it one of the most powerful tools in mechanics.

basics.text: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms (kg).
Velocity is speed in a given direction. It is measured in metres per second (m/s).
1000 g = 1 kg, so 50 g is 0.05 kg.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating momentum
keyPoints.content: Higher only: momentum is defined as the product of an object's mass and its velocity. The equation is: p = mv. Here p is momentum (kg m/s), m is mass (kg) and v is velocity (m/s). Momentum is a vector quantity. It has both magnitude and direction. So when two objects move in opposite directions, their momenta have opposite signs. Momentum is measured in kg m/s. Example: a 1,500 kg car travelling at 20 m/s has momentum = 1,500 × 20 = 30,000 kg m/s.
writeBullets: Momentum is a vector — has direction as well as magnitude
Objects moving in opposite directions have opposite signs of momentum
Example: 1,500 kg car at 20 m/s → p = 1,500 × 20 = 30,000 kg m/s

keyTerms.def: The product of an object's mass and velocity: p = mv; measured in kg m/s; a vector quantity with direction
A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction — e.g. momentum, velocity, force

keyPoints.memTip: p = mv. The unit is kg m/s. That is the same as mass × velocity units.

keyPoints.heading: Conservation of momentum
keyPoints.content: Higher only: the law of conservation of momentum applies to a closed system, with no outside forces. It says the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after. This applies to collisions and explosions. For a collision: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂. Here u is initial velocity and v is final velocity. For an explosion, like a gun firing: before the event, total momentum = 0, because everything is still. After the event, the bullet and gun move in opposite directions. Their momenta are equal in size and opposite in sign. So they still add up to zero. This is why a gun recoils when fired.
writeBullets: Conservation of momentum: total momentum before = total momentum after (closed system)
Collision equation: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂
Explosion: before = 0; after = equal and opposite momenta (sum still = 0)
Gun recoil: bullet goes forward (+), gun recoils backward (−), total = 0

keyTerms.def: In a closed system (no external forces), the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after
A system in which no external forces act, so momentum is conserved

keyPoints.memTip: Total momentum before = total momentum after, in a closed system.

keyPoints.heading: Force and change in momentum
keyPoints.content: Higher only: a resultant force acting on an object that is moving, or able to move, changes its momentum. The equations F = m × a and a = (v − u) / t combine to give F = m Δv / Δt. Here m Δv is the change in momentum, so force equals the rate of change of momentum. A bigger change in velocity, or a shorter time, means a bigger force. Rearranged: FΔt = Δp, so force × time = change in momentum. Compare a large force for a short time with a small force for a long time. Both can give the same change in momentum. This explains safety features. Air bags, seat belts, gymnasium crash mats, cycle helmets and cushioned playground surfaces all make an impact last longer. Crumple zones in cars do the same. A longer time means a smaller rate of change of momentum. So the force is smaller (same Δp, larger Δt → smaller F).
writeBullets: F = Δp / Δt (force = change in momentum ÷ time)
FΔt = Δp (force × time = change in momentum)
Larger time → smaller force for same change in momentum
Crumple zones, airbags: increase collision time → reduce force on passengers
Seat belts, crash mats, helmets, cushioned playground surfaces: same principle — extend the time of impact

keyTerms.def: The difference between final and initial momentum: Δp = mv − mu; caused by a resultant force acting over time

keyPoints.memTip: FΔt = Δp. Force × time = change in momentum.

0.question: A cyclist and bike have a mass of 70 kg and move at 6 m/s. What is their momentum?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. p = m v = 70 × 6 = 420 kg m/s.
0.wrongFeedback: Use p = m v. Multiply the mass by the velocity: 70 × 6 = 420. Momentum is measured in kg m/s, not newtons.

1.question: Two skaters stand still on the ice. They push each other apart. What is their total momentum just after the push?
options: Zero, just as it was before they pushed
Equal to the faster skater's momentum
Equal to the heavier skater's momentum
Twice the momentum of either skater
1.correctFeedback: Yes. The total was zero before, so it is zero after. The two skaters have equal momentum in opposite directions, so they cancel.
1.wrongFeedback: Before the push, nothing moves, so the total momentum is zero. Momentum is conserved, so the total is still zero after. The skaters move apart with equal momentum in opposite directions.

2.question: Why do crumple zones in cars reduce injury in a crash?
options: They reduce the total change in momentum during the collision
They increase the time of the collision, which reduces the force experienced by passengers
They make the car stop in a shorter time, which reduces the force
They increase the mass of the car, reducing deceleration
2.correctFeedback: Right. F = Δp/Δt. The change in momentum is fixed, because the speed change is the same. By increasing the time (Δt), the force (F) is reduced. Less force = less injury.
2.wrongFeedback: The change in momentum (Δp) in a crash is fixed. The car stops from a given speed. Crumple zones increase the TIME (Δt) over which the car decelerates. Using F = Δp/Δt: same Δp, larger Δt → smaller F. Smaller force on passengers → less injury. The total momentum change isn't reduced. It is the force that is reduced.

commonMistakes: Forgetting that momentum is a vector. In conservation problems, objects may move in opposite directions. Then one must be given a negative velocity. Getting this wrong gives the wrong answer.
Mixing up force × time (FΔt) and work done (Fd). FΔt gives a change in momentum and involves time. Work done involves distance.
In conservation of momentum calculations, adding masses instead of using them separately. When objects stick together in a collision, add the masses AFTER the collision, not before.
Saying crumple zones 'reduce momentum'. They don't. They increase the time of impact to reduce the force. The momentum change is the same.
examTips: For momentum calculations: (1) state p = mv. (2) Work out the momentum before the event. (3) Apply conservation. (4) Solve for the unknown. Show all steps.
For 'explain why crumple zones reduce injury': quote F = Δp/Δt and say that Δp is fixed. Explain that crumple zones increase Δt. Conclude that F decreases. This is the full mark scheme answer.
When objects move in opposite directions, assign one velocity as negative. This is vital for explosion questions, where the starting momentum = 0.
Units check: momentum is in kg m/s, force in N and time in s.
revisionCardBullets: Momentum: p = mv (mass × velocity); units = kg m/s
Momentum is a vector — has direction; opposite directions = opposite signs
Conservation of momentum: total before = total after (closed system)
Explosion from rest: before p = 0; after, the momenta of the parts still add up to zero
Force-momentum: F = Δp / Δt (force = change in momentum ÷ time)
FΔt = Δp (force × time = change in momentum)
Safety devices (crumple zones, airbags, helmets): increase collision time → reduce force
Same Δp, larger Δt → smaller F → less injury
